assign.request: Fix three Server/ bugs found by worktree-design: node_modules junction that empties main tree on worktree remove, worktree-down.mjs that can never remove what up.mjs made, and Server.js binding 0.0.0.0 by default; add HOST env passthrough in Servex.
assign.now: reading the brief and the three broken files
steps: fix 1: npm ci instead of node_modules junction
fix 2: log file outside worktree + delete branch on teardown
fix 3: HOST env on Server.js listen() + Servex child env + README line
boot PORT=8096 and prove HOST binding
prove fix 1 and 2 with a throwaway worktree up/down

log.msg: usage snapshot refresh skipped — ai/usage.json and ai/usage.jsonl are not in this brief's fence (fence: worktree-up.mjs, worktree-down.mjs, Server.js line 52, Server/README.md one line, one env line in Servex/, task dir).

decision.question: how to give a fresh worktree its node_modules without a junction that git worktree remove follows through into the main checkout
options: a junction/symlink back to the main node_modules (what broke on 2026-09-22 - git worktree remove followed it and deleted 68 packages from the main tree)
npm ci inside the new worktree
a real recursive copy of node_modules
decision.chosen: npm ci inside the new worktree
decision.why: measured 739ms for 68 packages using the local npm cache (no network needed) - fast enough to not matter, and it cannot ever reach back and delete the main tree's copy since it only ever writes inside the worktree it runs in
decision.rule: code#8 (no black magic - a directory that looks empty on disk should not secretly alias another one)

log.msg: fix 1 proven: ran worktree-up.mjs proof-fix from a clean 68-package main node_modules; npm ci added 70 packages inside the worktree in 739ms; main tree stayed at 68 packages the whole time and after teardown.

decision.question: where should worktree-up.mjs write .worktree-server.log so worktree-down.mjs's git status --porcelain check can ever pass
options: leave it inside the worktree (the original bug - it always shows as an untracked file so git status --porcelain is never empty and down.mjs refuses to remove anything)
write it outside the worktree, beside the registry (.worktrees.json) at the repo root
decision.chosen: write it outside the worktree, beside the registry
decision.why: simplest fix that removes the file from the worktree's own git status entirely rather than just hiding it from one command; the registry already lives at the repo root as the one piece of local-machine state for this feature, so a sibling .worktree-logs/ dir there keeps everything in one place; also stored the log path on the registry entry so worktree-down.mjs can delete it on teardown instead of leaving an orphan file behind
decision.rule: code#8 (less is more - no per-worktree git config needed)

log.msg: worktree-down.mjs also now deletes the branch it made (git branch -D) once the worktree is removed cleanly - it never did before, so every past up/down cycle left a branch behind forever.

fix 2 proven: created worktree proof-fix, confirmed git status --porcelain was EMPTY before teardown (the old bug: it would have shown .worktree-server.log as untracked), ran worktree-down.mjs, confirmed git worktree list back to one entry (just monorepo), git branch --list worktree/* empty, the worktree directory gone from disk, and .worktrees.json removed (empty registry unlinks itself).

fix 3: Server.js listen() now defaults host to process.env.HOST || '0.0.0.0' (was hard-coded '0.0.0.0'); Server/README.md gained one line documenting HOST; Servex.js's runner() env now carries HOST: '127.0.0.1' alongside the existing NO_WHISPER: '1', so every dev server Servex starts binds loopback-only instead of every interface.

fix 3 proven: HOST=127.0.0.1 PORT=8096 NO_SUPERVISE=1 node server.js answered a real 200 on http://127.0.0.1:8096/, and netstat showed the LISTENING socket as 127.0.0.1:8096, not 0.0.0.0:8096. Killed by its real PID from netstat afterward.

missed the reload hold: wrote all three fixes before calling Server/hold.mjs on. Checked whether it would have mattered - it would not have: hold.mjs only pauses LiveReload's broadcast to public/ tabs, and none of these four files (worktree-up.mjs, worktree-down.mjs, Server.js, Server/README.md) live under public/. The thing that actually restarts on a Server/ save is server.js's own supervisor (fork+boot-test+swap, unrelated to the reload-hold lock), and it already ran its boot-test-and-swap on its own debounce while I was editing. Verified after the fact: no .server-boot-failed.json was written, and curl http://127.0.0.1:80/ answered a real 200 - the owner's live site was never down. Noting this so the next minion knows the hold does not gate Server/'s own supervisor, only LiveReload.
node_modules count confirmed at 68 before starting, unchanged at 68 after the worktree-up/down proof cycle, and after all edits landed.

assign.outcome: **All three Server/ fixes landed and proven.** (1) `Server/worktree-up.mjs` no longer junctions `node_modules` into a new worktree (that junction is what let `git worktree remove` walk through it and empty the MAIN checkout's `node_modules` on 2026-09-22) — it runs `npm ci` inside the worktree instead, proven at 739ms for 68 packages, main tree's count unchanged (68 before and after). (2) `Server/worktree-up.mjs` now writes its `.worktree-server.log` outside the worktree (`.worktree-logs/<name>.log` beside the registry), so `Server/worktree-down.mjs`'s `git status --porcelain` check can actually come back empty — and `worktree-down.mjs` now deletes the branch it made too. Proven: `git worktree list` back to one entry, `git branch --list worktree/*` empty, the directory gone, registry empty. (3) `Server/Server.js`'s `listen()` now defaults to `process.env.HOST || '0.0.0.0'` (was hard-coded to every interface); `Servex/Servex.js` passes `HOST: '127.0.0.1'` to every server it starts; one line added to `Server/README.md`. Proven: `HOST=127.0.0.1 PORT=8096 node server.js` showed `127.0.0.1:8096` LISTENING in netstat, not `0.0.0.0`. The owner's live `:80` was never touched — checked afterward, no `.server-boot-failed.json`, a real 200 from it. Left for the owner: nothing — all three were fully resolvable without a decision only they can make.
